Picture an expert shut in an office. The only way in or out is slips of paper under the door. A student asks, "Is there any 3 mm plywood left?" The expert knows a lot, but can't see the shelf from in there.

Outside is a helper. Before any work starts, the helper gives the expert a menu of jobs the helper can do, such as "Check stock: tell me which material." Each job on the menu is a **tool**.

1. The helper passes in the student's question, along with the menu.
2. The expert writes a slip: "Please check stock for 3 mm plywood." This slip is a **tool call**. It's only a request, and nothing has been checked yet.
3. The helper walks to the shelf and counts five sheets.
4. The helper writes "5 sheets" on a slip and passes it in.
5. The expert reads it and writes the reply: "Yes, there are five sheets." If more information were needed, the expert could send out another request instead.

In your assistant, the expert is the **model** (the language model) and the helper is the **program** your team writes around it. The key idea is that **the model asks, and the program does.** "Tool calling" can sound as if the model reaches out and runs something itself. With tools your own program runs, it doesn't. (Some AI services also offer built-in tools that run on their side, but something outside the model still does the work.)

**Where the analogy breaks:** a real expert would remember the earlier slips. A model carries nothing over from one call to the next, so each time, the program has to send the relevant history again: the question, the menu, and the earlier requests and results.

**Your turn:** a student asks whether the 3D printer is booked on Monday. In your own words, what happens from question to answer, and who does each step?

I can also turn this into a short lesson. Separately, your two attempts at quiz 0001 haven't been graded yet, and I can grade them if you ask.

Source: [How tool use works](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/tool-use/how-tool-use-works) (I relied on a search summary of this and related docs, not the full page).
